title: Asma bint Abi Bakr
hook: she of the two belts, who stood firm before a tyrant

segments.voice: Yesterday: Nusaybah, who stood her ground at Uhud. Your line was she stood her ground.

A bag of food, a skin of water, and nothing to tie them shut. Two men are about to slip out of Mecca in secret, and the provisions have to travel. The one packing them is the daughter of one of the two men. No cord, no strap, nothing. So she reaches for the cloth tied around her own waist. Decades later, a powerful man will try to use that moment to mock her son. It won't go the way he planned. Today: Asma, daughter of Abu Bakr.
screen: `FOOD, WATER, NOTHING TO TIE THEM.` → `SHE REACHES FOR HER OWN BELT.` → `DECADES LATER, A TAUNT.`

segments.voice: Sahih al-Bukhari tells the first half. When the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, and Abu Bakr set out from Mecca for Medina, Asma prepared their food for the road. She could find nothing to tie the food bag and the water skin, so she cut her waistband in two, tied the food with one half and the water with the other, and from then on she was called she of the two belts. Sahih Muslim tells the second half, many years on. Her son, Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr, has been killed in Mecca by the forces of al-Hajjaj, the governor. Al-Hajjaj sends for his mother. She refuses. He sends again, with threats. She still refuses. So he goes to her and asks how she sees what he did to her son. She answers that he ruined her son's world, and her son ruined his hereafter. Then she picks up the insult he had been using. You call him the son of the woman of the two belts. Yes, I am she of the two belts. With one I tied up the food of the Messenger of God and of Abu Bakr. The other is the belt no woman does without. And she tells him a saying she heard from the Prophet, about a liar and a destroyer who would come from the tribe of Thaqif, and says plainly that she thinks the governor is the destroyer. The report says he got up and left without answering. Tradition remembers her as very old by then.
screen: `SHE CUT HER WAISTBAND IN TWO.` · `THE GOVERNOR SENDS; SHE REFUSES.` · `YES, I AM SHE OF THE TWO BELTS.` · `HE LEFT WITHOUT AN ANSWER.` · then, large: `SHE OF THE TWO BELTS.`

segments.voice: This week ran from Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas and his third, through Abu Ubaydah, Khalid, Abu Sufyan and Hind, Ikrimah and Nusaybah, to Asma. Bring to mind someone old whom you've watched stay steady, a grandparent, a neighbor, a teacher, and then yourself, older than you are now: what would you want to still be holding? If you pray, you can ask for steadiness in your later years.
Asma, who cut her belt in two for the Prophet's journey, and held up that very name, years later, in front of a governor. Today's word.
Your line: she of the two belts. The name meant to shame her son became her answer. That's day eight hundred forty-seven.

howItsDone: Muslims tell Asma's story from Sahih al-Bukhari, where she cuts her belt for the journey to Medina, and Sahih Muslim, where she faces al-Hajjaj after her son's death.

chat.says: Why was Asma called she of the two belts?
options: She cut her waistband in two to tie up the food and water for the journey.
She wore two belts as a sign of marrying into a noble family.
The Prophet gave her two belts as thanks for hiding him in a cave.
chat.meaning: Bukhari: she found nothing to tie the food bag and water skin, so she cut her waistband in two. Years later she held the name up to al-Hajjaj.

Asma.meaning: Abu Bakr's daughter, called she of the two belts

Abu Bakr.meaning: the Prophet's close friend, who traveled with him to Medina

al-Hajjaj.meaning: the governor whose forces killed Asma's son

Thaqif.meaning: a tribe named in the Prophet's saying
